title: Good Schools Don't Beat Staff Turnover
author: Robert Pondiscio
summary: Pondiscio argues that education's real problem is not finding successful schools, it is sustaining them, because turnover among superintendents, principals, and teachers is not a defect to be engineered away but a permanent feature of the system. Drawing on his reporting on Success Academy in How the Other Half Learns, he contends that durable schools look less like a teacher corps of lifers and more like the US military: a small officer class surrounding a rotating base of enlisted staff executing a clearly defined operating model. The institutional features he associates with durability are a common instructional core with observable definitions of effective teaching, ruthless consistency in foundational literacy and numeracy delivery, and coaching and walkthroughs that correct drift before it becomes culture. Pondiscio explicitly rejects charismatic principals, compelling origin stories, and current test scores as predictors of longevity, and he flags that Success Academy's model may not be portable outside labor markets full of ambitious young adults willing to grind for a few years. The provocation he leaves leaders with is that if your model only works while the adults stay in place, it is not really a model, it is lightning in a bottle, and the next decade of reform should be about studying Stockton-and-Ripken-style institutional durability rather than chasing the next Jordan.
points: Average superintendent tenure is roughly one contract cycle, principals last about four years per school (less in high-poverty settings), and about a third of teachers leave the classroom within five years, so turnover is structural not aberrational.
Chad Alderman's Virginia data show only half of 2004 top-quartile schools were still top-quartile in 2024, suggesting school-level success is far more fragile than current-year test scores imply.

Durability correlates with a defined instructional core (not a philosophy), standardized materials, common sequencing, observable definitions of effective teaching, and active drift correction via walkthroughs and coaching.

Success Academy's results despite heavy staff turnover suggest the operating model, not staff stability, is what carries performance, though Pondiscio cautions the model may not transfer to smaller or less attractive labor markets.

Research and emulation effort should shift from celebrating current high-fliers to identifying schools and districts that have sustained results for a decade or more, particularly with statistically disadvantaged students.
quotes: When successful schools lose their momentum, the usual suspects are leadership turnover, staff churn, demographic change, political conflict, or the quiet assumption that the success was fragile all along. But many of these factors, particularly staff and leadership changes, are not flaws in our system, they're features.

Any school improvement model that only works if the adults stay in place isn't a model. It's catching lightning in a bottle. What ultimately distinguishes the schools that endure is not whether turnover happens, but whether effective practices have been institutionalized strongly enough to survive it.

Durable schools tend to share a clearly defined instructional core. Not a "philosophy." Not a mission statement. An operating system. They use common materials, sequence content deliberately, and define effective instruction in observable terms. New teachers are acculturated and trained into an existing model rather than invited to invent their own.
Fragile systems rely on great teachers. Durable systems assume ordinary teachers and build routines strong enough to support them. Durable systems assume turnover and design accordingly.

The de facto model that has evolved is more like the U.S. Army or the Marines: a small and talented officer corps surrounded by enlisted men and women who do a tour, maybe two, then muster out, with new recruits reporting for duty. Teacher turnover, lack of experience and continuity, is widely assumed to be a problem, particularly in urban schools. But it's never suggested that our military would be better if only soldiers stayed in uniform longer.

Looking back, education reform spent decades searching for the miracle school, the visionary leader, the transformative model, the "It's Being Done" proof point that dramatic improvement was possible. We found many such schools. What we rarely built were institutions designed to sustain their promising results.” Archived from The Next 30 Years (Substack) on April 21, 2026 by Tim.
